newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: EU seeks East European help against drugs scourge.
newsitem.headline: EU seeks East European help against drugs scourge.

text.p: European Union leaders sought to enlist the help of their east European counterparts on Saturday in a new drive against the drugs scourge ruining lives from Athens to Amsterdam.

EU leaders, on the last day of the Dublin summit, pressed counterparts from 10 East European states seeking EU membership to crack down on the growing export of opiates and heroin across their frontiers.
They had lunch with their East European guests and then discussed the EU's plan to fight crime, terrorism and drug trafficking and to try to make it an international action.
"The lunch was entirely given over to the fight against terrorism and organised crime and drugs," French President Jacques Chirac told reporters.
Three or four of the 10 - the Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland and Slovenia - are tipped to be among the first wave of new EU members when it embarks on enlargement.
"One of the essential tasks of enlargement will be to harmonise legislation sufficiently to eradicate this major danger (drugs and crime) which is becoming increasingly urgent," said Chirac.

The meeting took place as the EU summit unveiled a concerted attack on crime and drugs through better police and customs coordination -- a priority in Dublin's six month presidency of the EU which ends on December 31.
Irish officials said a similar crackdown in the Balkans and Eastern Europe would bolster the EU action and found broad backing from their guests.
"We tried to focus on cooperation, such as helping them develop their law enforcement agencies," said one Irish official who attended the meeting.
"Our cooperation programmes could be focused on developing the kind of law enforcement that will deter drug traffic," said another.

Western drug agencies say that an increasing amount of opiates and heroin cultivated in the Asian subcontinent and elsewhere is finding its way to European users across what used to be the iron curtain.
They are especially concerned about the amount of opiates seeping into EU drug networks through what used to be called the "silk road" from Afghanistan towards Moscow and western Europe.
There is also evidence of raw heroin reaching western Europe through the Balkans, drug agencies say.

Under communism, draconian legislation outlawed drug trafficking in Eastern Europe but there has been an explosion of crime and narcotics trade since the fall of the Berlin wall and the adoption of free market systems, drug agencies say.
The 10 East European leaders exchanged views on how their applications to join the EU are proceeding and the development of their economies and political systems for membership.
Countries represented were Romania, Bulgaria, the Czech republic, Hungary, Poland, Slovenia, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania and Slovakia. Cyprus was also present.
